questions.q: The chapter compares Indian culture with some other ancient cultures that were diluted or even destroyed over time. Which group of cultures does it name?
questions.a: Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and Rome
o: Greece, Persia, Central Asia and East Asia
Egypt, Persia, Rome and Central Asia

questions.q: A 13th-century chronicle from a north Indian town notes three things that arrived with the town's new rulers: a new way of running provinces and collecting taxes, a new style of building, and a new way of looking at the world. Which statement about these three fits the chapter?
questions.a: All three fit what the chapter says rulers from the early 13th century brought: administrative systems, architectural styles and a different worldview
o: All three fit what the chapter says rulers from the early 13th century brought: administrative systems, architectural styles and a different worldview
None of them fits; the chapter says the new rulers brought only new religious beliefs
Only the new style of building fits; the chapter says new administrative systems came with merchants and traders from ancient times
They show that from the 13th century India stopped adopting or adapting cultural currents from outside

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter mean by 'culture'? (b) Name any two things that, according to the chapter, culture includes.
questions.a: (a) Culture is the shared way of life that defines a group of people, often passed down through generations; it shapes how people see the world, interact with each other and conduct their daily lives. (b) Any two of: values, morals, customs, traditions, art, music, literature, philosophy, science.
s: (a) The shared way of life of a group of people, passed down through generations
(b) Any two correct items, such as values and music

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Indian culture has been one of the most resilient cultures, standing strong through the ages while some other ancient cultures were diluted or destroyed.
Reason (R): Visitors came to India from Greece, Persia, Central Asia and East Asia, carrying their own social norms, cuisine, language and religion.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Mohan writes in his notes: 'Wherever Muslim rulers governed in the 13th to 17th centuries, Persian and Arabic influences simply replaced the local culture.' Test Mohan's claim against the chapter. Give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: Mohan's claim is wrong. (1) The chapter says that under the patronage of the ruling Muslim class in several parts, Persian and Arabic influences were witnessed in various aspects of the local culture, often creating new art forms: they mixed with the local culture instead of replacing it. (2) It names continuation of traditional practices in Indian communities as a common pattern of the whole period, and says Indian culture continued to grow ever richer and proved remarkably strong and adaptable.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong; the influences mixed in, they did not replace local culture
Reason 1: Persian and Arabic influences appeared in aspects of local culture, often creating new art forms
Reason 2: traditional practices continued and culture grew richer, strong and adaptable

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) Name any two kinds of visitors who came to India from ancient times. (b) Name any two regions they came from. (c) Name any two things they carried with them. (d) In which century does the chapter say a new chapter in India's history began, when rulers brought new political ideas and a different worldview? (e) According to the chapter, what happened to these visitors after India welcomed them, and who gained from it?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: merchants and traders, knowledge-seekers and scholars, diplomats, people persecuted in their homeland. (b) Any two of: Greece, Persia, Central Asia, East Asia. (c) Any two of: social norms, cuisine, food habits, fashion, jewellery, art, language, literature, religion, festivals. (d) The early 13th century. (e) They assimilated into Indian society, benefiting both India and the visitors.
s: (a) Two kinds of visitors, such as merchants and diplomats
(b) Two regions, such as Greece and Persia
(c) Two things carried, such as cuisine and language
(d) The early 13th century
(e) They assimilated into Indian society, benefiting both

questions.q: In which part of India does the chapter place the bhakti saints Tukaram, Dnyaneshwar and Namdev?
questions.a: The west

questions.q:
Match each bhakti saint in Column A with the region the chapter links them to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Mirabai 2. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu 3. Kanakadasa 4. Kabirdas
Column B: P. The south Q. Present-day Uttar Pradesh R. Rajasthan S. The east
A Sufi practises zikr. What is he doing, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Chanting or silently reciting divine names to remember God
o: Chanting or silently reciting divine names to remember God
Whirling round and round as a dance before an audience
Singing a qawwali that fuses local and Sufi musical styles
Giving up all worldly desires and possessions for the rest of life

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter describes Sufism as a path that grew up outside Islam.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter describes Sufism as a path of Islam that focuses on devotion and an inner and personal search for god.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Sufism is a path of Islam focused on devotion and an inner, personal search for god

questions.q: A museum shows a late 17th-century painting of Kabirdas, who lived in the 15th century, surrounded by attendants of many different kinds. (a) About how long after Kabir's lifetime was the painting made? (b) What does the chapter say such late paintings of the saints show? (c) What does the variety among Kabir's attendants suggest, linked to what the chapter says about his message?
questions.a: (a) About two centuries after his lifetime (15th century to late 17th century). (b) The chapter says some paintings were made almost two centuries after the lives of the sants, showing that their influence continued much longer; their bhajans are still sung today. (c) His message reached many kinds of people: his compositions spoke of one god, decried the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam, appealed to many people and became popular, and people from all sections of society took part in bhajan gatherings.
s: (a) About two centuries later
(b) The saints' influence continued long after their lives; their bhajans are still sung
(c) His message of one god, against the rituals of both religions, appealed to people of all sections of society

questions.q:
A cultural society in Ajmer plans a 60-minute evening on devotion in the 13th to 17th centuries. Each item takes 20 minutes, so only three of its four proposals can be staged. P1: Kabir's dohas sung as bhajans with instruments, in a local language. P2: a qawwali sung in the manner of the Sufi saints. P3: a recitation of the Divya Prabandham in Tamil. P4: hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib.
(a) Which group of Tamil devotees composed the hymns of P3, and in which centuries were such hymns composed?
(b) According to the chapter, why did Sufi saints sing songs like P2, and what did they fuse in them?
(c) Whose teachings does the text in P4 preserve, and whose hymns are preserved with them?
(d) The society wants the evening to show that the bhakti and Sufi traditions often overlapped. Which proposal should it drop? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Alvars; the hymns were composed between the 6th and 9th centuries. (b) To bring people closer to the divine; they fused local classical musical styles with their own. (c) Guru Nanak's teachings, preserved along with the hymns of several Hindu saints. (d) Drop P3. It shows how an old Tamil tradition stayed alive, but it was composed centuries before this period and has no link to Sufi practice. P1 (Kabir's one god, against the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam), P2 (Sufi qawwali) and P4 (Guru Nanak's one God, with Hindu saints' hymns in one text) together show different paths meeting.
s: (a) The Alvars, 6th to 9th centuries
(b) To bring people closer to the divine, fusing local classical styles with their own
(c) Guru Nanak's teachings with the hymns of several Hindu saints
(d) Drops P3, explaining that it shows continuity but not bhakti-Sufi overlap, while P1, P2 and P4 show the paths meeting

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Devotional traditions such as the Alvar and Nayanar hymns kept thriving through long periods of political turmoil.
Reason (R): The chapter says these devotional developments thrived only because Hindu and Muslim rulers gave them patronage.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: In which two related streams did Indian classical music develop, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Hindustani in the North and Carnatic in the South
o: Hindustani in the North and Carnatic in the South
Carnatic in the North and Hindustani in the South
Dhrupad in the North and qawwali in the South
Hindustani in the East and Carnatic in the West

questions.q: The name 'dhrupad' comes from two words, dhruva and pada. What do these words mean, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Fixed and verse

questions.q:
Match each person in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Raja Mansingh Tomar 2. Tansen 3. Amir Khusrau 4. Purandaradasa
Column B: P. Called the father of Carnatic music Q. Credited with developing the qawwali R. Patron in Gwalior under whom dhrupad reached new heights S. Became one of the nine ratnas of Akbar's court
(a) What do the two parts of the word 'pattachitra' mean? (b) Name one state where the chapter says pattachitra was found, and the kind of stories it usually showed.
questions.a: (a) Patta means 'cloth' and chitra means 'picture', so a pattachitra is a cloth picture. (b) Odisha, West Bengal or Andhra Pradesh; it usually showed scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas.
s: (a) Patta = cloth and chitra = picture
(b) One of Odisha, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, and scenes from the epics or Puranas

questions.q: True or False? 'Amir Khusrau, who developed the qawwali, could have sung together with Tansen at Akbar's court.' Give the verdict and the reason, using the dates the chapter gives.
questions.a: False. The chapter says Amir Khusrau lived from the mid-13th century to the early 14th century, while its portrait of Tansen, who went to Akbar's court, dates from about 1585. The two lived more than two centuries apart.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: Khusrau lived from the mid-13th to the early 14th century, Tansen in the late 16th century (portrait of about 1585), more than two centuries apart

questions.q: A music teacher sums up classical music of this period as 'one root, two branches, and outside influences on only one branch'. Explain in three points how the chapter supports each part of her image.
questions.a: (1) One root: the chapter calls Hindustani and Carnatic music two related streams of one Indian classical music, and music has been part of Indian culture since ancient times. (2) Two branches: Hindustani music developed in the North and Carnatic music in the South. (3) Outside influences on one branch: in the North, Tansen was influenced by a Sufi saint and Amir Khusrau's qawwali fused Indian, Persian and Arabic singing traditions, while Carnatic music continued to develop independently, largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influences.
s: One root: the two streams are related and grew from one old tradition
Two branches: Hindustani in the North, Carnatic in the South
Outside influences on one branch: Persian or Sufi influence in the North (Tansen or Amir Khusrau) while Carnatic music stayed largely unaffected

questions.q: Classify each development below as showing continuity, change, or both, with one reason from the chapter for each. (a) Dhrupad under Raja Mansingh Tomar of Gwalior. (b) Tansen's compositions. (c) The sitar and the tabla. (d) Carnatic music in this period. (e) Using (a) to (d), explain what the chapter means when it says Indian culture could 'accept influences and enrich itself while retaining its core'.
questions.a: (a) Both: dhrupad was a genre of great antiquity (continuity) that was developed to new heights in the late 15th century under Raja Mansingh Tomar's patronage (change). (b) Both: Tansen was influenced by a Sufi saint, which shows in some of his compositions, while he also continued to compose in praise of Krishna and Shiva. (c) Both: their modern forms evolved through experimentation by makers and musicians of various backgrounds, but their repertoires came from much older Indian instruments, such as the pakhawaj for the tabla. (d) Continuity: Carnatic music continued to develop independently, largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influences. (Both is also accepted if the student explains that it kept developing on its own (change) without outside influence (continuity).) (e) Music took in new elements, such as Sufi influence and new instrument forms, yet kept its old genres, devotional themes and repertoires, so it grew richer without losing its core.
s: (a) Both: an ancient genre (continuity) developed to new heights (change)
(b) Both: Sufi influence alongside songs in praise of Krishna and Shiva
(c) Both: new forms through experimentation, repertoire from older instruments such as the pakhawaj
(d) Continuity: developed largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influences (accept Both: kept developing on its own, without outside influence)
(e) Explains that new influences were absorbed while old genres and repertoires were kept

questions.q: The chapter uses the word 'atelier' for the place where Akbar's painters worked. What is an atelier?
questions.a: An artist's studio
o: A wall painting in a palace

questions.q: A museum receives three paintings in the Rajput style, each showing traditional Hindu themes. Painting P is dated 1350, Painting Q is dated 1610 and Painting R is dated 1880. Which of these dates fall within the period in which the chapter says the Rajput painting tradition was thriving?
questions.a: Q and R only

questions.q:
Read the statements about miniature painting.
I. The Rajput painting tradition thrived from the 15th century to the late 19th century.
II. Mughal miniature painting mainly showed traditional Hindu themes such as lotus flowers and banyan trees.
III. Some Mughal court painters migrated to Bikaner, leading to a blending of styles.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: A painting from 1598 shows Yudhishthira and Karna wrestling. (a) From which work does the chapter say this folio comes, and what is that work? (b) Who commissioned the work?
questions.a: (a) The Razmnama, a Persian translation of the Mahabharata. (b) Akbar.
s: (a) The Razmnama, a Persian translation of the Mahabharata
(b) Akbar

questions.q: Answer in three short parts about miniature painting. (a) Name any two early forms of painting that the chapter mentions from before paintings were made on paper. (b) In which century did paper reach India, according to the chapter? (c) Name any two themes that Mughal miniature paintings depicted.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: cave art, the Ajanta murals, murals and frescoes. (b) The 10th or 11th century. (c) Any two of: landscapes, court scenes, portraits (secular themes).
s: (a) Any two of cave art, the Ajanta murals, murals and frescoes
(b) The 10th or 11th century
(c) Any two of landscapes, court scenes, portraits

questions.q:
A heritage trust in Rajasthan studies the order book of a 17th-century court painting workshop (the figures are illustrative). Period 1, before some Mughal-trained painters joined the workshop: the raja ordered 30 paintings, 24 of epic and devotional scenes and 6 of hunting or court scenes. Period 2, after they joined: he ordered 40 paintings, 22 of epic and devotional scenes and 18 of hunting or court scenes with garden plants and animals.
(a) According to the chapter, on what was the inclusion of such new elements in Rajput paintings based?
(b) To which place does the chapter say some Mughal court painters migrated, leading to a blending of styles?
(c) Find the share of hunting or court scenes in each period, as a percentage.
(d) A trust member says the new hunting and court scenes took the place of the old epic and devotional scenes. Use the counts and the chapter to decide whether the new scenes mainly replaced the old ones or were mainly added to them.
questions.a: (a) The patrons' taste and demand. (b) Bikaner. (c) Period 1: 6 of 30 = 20%; Period 2: 18 of 40 = 45%. (d) They were mainly added. Hunting and court scenes rose by 12 (from 6 to 18), but epic and devotional scenes fell by only 2 (from 24 to 22), while the total grew by 10 (from 30 to 40). So the member is wrong: the workshop took in new elements and still kept painting the old themes, which fits the chapter's statement that the traditional Hindu themes of the Rajput style continued to flourish.
s: (a) The patrons' taste and demand
(b) Bikaner
(c) 20% in Period 1 and 45% in Period 2
(d) Mainly added: +12 new scenes against -2 old ones, so the old themes continued to flourish

questions.q: Which words for gardens does the chapter say are mentioned in the Rigveda, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana?
questions.a: Udyana, vatika and nandana

questions.q: Two 17th-century gardens in different kingdoms both follow the geometrical pattern of the Mughal gardens, with water channels. Yet they look quite different: one is built of the local stone of its region by craftsmen trained in local traditions, and the other is shaped to suit the taste of the raja who paid for it. Which feature of the time, described in the chapter, does this fit?
questions.a: The evolution of localised forms, based on the patron ruler's taste, local traditions and materials, and the craftsmen's expertise
o: The evolution of localised forms, based on the patron ruler's taste, local traditions and materials, and the craftsmen's expertise
The exact copying of the Persian charbagh design everywhere, without any change
The use of water channels only for irrigation, never as aesthetic elements
The end of India's older garden tradition once the Mughals arrived

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Visitors in India today can still see gardens laid out in the Mughal style.
Reason (R): The Mughal-style gardens developed around forts, tombs and mosques continue to exist today.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name any two features that the chapter says Mughal gardens included. (b) Name any two kinds of buildings around which such gardens were developed.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: water channels, fountains, terraces (laid out in four parts with gardens and waterways). (b) Any two of: forts, tombs, mosques.
s: (a) Two features, such as water channels and fountains
(b) Two kinds of buildings, such as forts and tombs

questions.q: Show, using the chapter, that the garden at Amer Fort cannot have been the model from which the Mughal garden style was copied.
questions.a: (1) The chapter dates the Amer Fort garden to the 17th century and says it borrowed elements from the Mughal gardens. (2) It followed the geometrical patterns of the Mughal gardens, with water channels, so the Mughal pattern already existed for it to follow. (3) The Mughal style itself came from the Persian charbagh design brought with the arrival of the Mughals, so the borrowing ran from Mughal gardens to Amer, not the other way.
s: States that the chapter says the 17th-century Amer garden borrowed from Mughal gardens
Explains that following the Mughal geometrical pattern means that pattern existed first
States that the Mughal style came from the Persian charbagh, so the borrowing ran from Mughal gardens to Amer

questions.q:
In 2026, a Class 8 heritage club in Madurai surveys two gardens for a school project. Garden A is an old garden around a temple, beside a stone tank. Garden B is a newer park laid out in four equal parts, divided by two crossing water channels, with fountains and low terraces. The club's note says that Garden B copies a design from Persia.
(a) Which old Indian tradition of gardens does Garden A follow, according to the chapter?
(b) Name the Persian garden design that Garden B copies.
(c) In that design, what do the gardens and waterways represent?
(d) With whose arrival does the chapter say gardens in India took on this new dimension?
questions.a: (a) The old tradition of gardens built around temples with a pond or a tank (gardens are mentioned in the Rigveda, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana). (b) The charbagh design. (c) The rivers of Paradise mentioned in the Quran. (d) The arrival of the Mughals.
s: (a) Gardens built around temples with a pond or tank
(b) The charbagh design
(c) The rivers of Paradise mentioned in the Quran
(d) The Mughals

questions.q: 'Purdah' is a Persian word. What does it mean, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Curtain or veil

questions.q: Whose account of the Vijayanagara court describes women who wrestled, women astrologers, women who wrote the accounts and women musicians on the king's staff?
questions.a: Fernao Nunes, a Portuguese traveller
o: Pietro Della Valle, an Italian traveller
Abu Zaidu-l Hasan, an Arab chronicler

questions.q: The chapter says that women engaged with the royal family were educated and accomplished in the arts, and that some were poets. (a) Name the woman poet at Achyutadevaraya's court whom the chapter introduces, and the Sanskrit kavya she wrote. (b) How does her example support the chapter's statement about women of royal families?
questions.a: (a) Tirumalamba, who wrote Varadambika Parinaya, a kavya in Sanskrit on the wedding of Achyutadevaraya and Princess Varadambika. (b) She was a celebrated poet at a royal court writing a full Sanskrit kavya, which shows that a woman connected with the royal family was educated, accomplished in the arts and a poet.
s: (a) Tirumalamba and Varadambika Parinaya
(b) Links her court poetry in Sanskrit to royal women being educated, accomplished and poets

questions.q: True or False? 'Nur Jahan's influence in the Mughal Empire went beyond the palace: she took an active part in governance.' Give the verdict and one piece of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: True. In the early 17th century Nur Jahan, wife of Emperor Jahangir, played an active role in governance: she issued royal orders and attended court meetings, and coins were minted in her name.
s: Verdict: True
Evidence: she issued royal orders, attended court meetings, or coins were minted in her name

questions.q: Explain, as a chain of three links, how the chapter connects the invasions from the 12th century onwards with the spread of purdah.
questions.a: (1) Invasions and military campaigns from the 12th century onwards led to women and children being imprisoned and sold as slaves in the markets of West and Central Asia, and some women committed jauhar. (2) As a consequence, attempts were made to protect women from this fate, and their public appearance and engagement declined. (3) Practices such as purdah became more widespread in certain regions, and in parts of north India the ghunghat became part of attire as a way of avoiding the public eye.
s: Link 1: women and children imprisoned and sold as slaves; some women committed jauhar
Link 2: attempts to protect women, so their public appearance and engagement declined
Link 3: purdah more widespread in certain regions; ghunghat in parts of north India

questions.q: A student plans to write: 'In the 13th to 17th centuries, purdah was the rule for women all over India.' She collects four sources from the chapter. S1: the Portuguese traveller Fernao Nunes's account of the women on the Vijayanagara king's staff. S2: the wall engravings at Hampi. S3: the note that in parts of north India the veil (ghunghat) became part of women's attire. S4: the note on women in royal Muslim households. Answer in four steps. (i) Name any three vocations of women that S1 records. (ii) Sort the four sources into those that fit her claim and those that go against it. (iii) What does the region of each group tell you? (iv) Decide whether her claim stands, and rewrite it so that it fits all four sources.
questions.a: (i) Any three of: women who wrestle; astrologers and soothsayers; women who write the accounts of expenses incurred inside the gates; women who write the affairs of the kingdom and compare their books with the writers outside; women who play instruments and sing. (ii) Fit the claim: S3, and S4 (women in royal Muslim households were generally secluded and followed purdah). Go against it: S1, and S2 (the engravings show women taking part in many activities of public life). (iii) The two that fit describe parts of north India and royal Muslim households; the two that go against it come from Vijayanagara in the south. This matches the chapter: the veiling system was largely confined to north India, with not much evidence of it elsewhere, and in south India the situation of women mostly did not change. (iv) The claim does not stand, because it holds for only one region. A fair version: 'In this period purdah and the veil spread in parts of north India, while in the south elite women went on taking part in public life.'
s: (i) Any three vocations from Nunes's account
(ii) S3 and S4 fit; S1 and S2 go against
(iii) The supporting sources are from north India, the opposing ones from Vijayanagara; veiling was largely confined to north India
(iv) Rejects the all-India claim and rewrites it as a regional one

questions.q:
A group of history students in 2026 studies 20 temple inscriptions from this period, copied in a museum (the figures are illustrative). 6 record queens or rich women donating entire villages to temples. 4 record wells and 2 record community halls built at the initiative of women. The other 8 record gifts by men.
(a) According to the chapter, what did a temple receive from a village donated to it?
(b) What percentage of the 20 inscriptions record a gift or a building by women?
(c) For whom does the chapter say the wells and community halls built at women's initiative were meant, and what does this show about these women?
(d) What conclusion does the chapter draw about women and the economy of this period? Explain how the inscriptions support it.
questions.a: (a) A part of the crop cultivated in the village was the temple's share. (b) 6 + 4 + 2 = 12 of the 20 inscriptions, that is 60%. (c) They were all for public use, which shows that these women took part in public life and served the whole community, not only their own households. (d) The chapter concludes that economic prosperity in this period could not have reached the heights it did without the active participation of women; women who could give away entire villages and pay for wells and halls clearly held wealth and used it in economic and public life.
s: (a) A part of the crop cultivated was the temple's share
(b) 12 of 20, that is 60%
(c) All for public use, so the women took part in public life
(d) Prosperity could not have reached its heights without women's active participation, backed by their wealth shown in the donations

questions.q: What does the chapter call the schools that villages had in this period?
questions.a: Pathashalas

questions.q: In 1350, a student must choose between Nalanda and Kanchipuram for advanced study of philosophy and mathematics. Which choice and reason fit the chapter?
questions.a: Kanchipuram, because it was renowned in the South for advanced learning in these subjects, while Nalanda had been destroyed in the late 12th century
o: Kanchipuram, because it was renowned in the South for advanced learning in these subjects, while Nalanda had been destroyed in the late 12th century
Nalanda, because it was still the leading university for philosophy and mathematics in the 14th century
Nalanda, because it was rebuilt soon after the invasions of the late 12th century
Neither, because the chapter says advanced learning stopped everywhere after the invasions

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Koshtis 2. Brocade 3. Pashmina 4. Geographical Indication (GI) tag
Column B: P. A rich fabric with a raised pattern, typically in gold or silver thread Q. The broad umbrella of ancient weaving communities R. Woven from the cashmere wool of goats of Ladakh and Kashmir S. Limits who can call a sari 'Banarasi'
(a) Name any two subjects that students studied in gurukulas, mathas, temple schools, viharas and pallis. (b) Name any two languages in which madrasas offered instruction under Muslim rule.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: Sanskrit and Prakrit grammar, astronomy, law, medicine, sacred texts. (b) Any two of: Arabic, Persian, Hindavi (madrasas also taught Islamic studies).
s: (a) Two subjects, such as astronomy and law
(b) Two languages, such as Arabic and Persian

questions.q: True or False? 'A pupil in a 16th-century madrasa who learned Hindavi was learning a language whose grammar came from Indian languages, even though it also used words from Persian and Arabic.' Give the verdict and the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. Under Muslim rule madrasas offered instruction in Arabic, Persian, Hindavi and Islamic studies, and the chapter explains Hindavi as an early version of the Hindi-Urdu language with the grammatical structure and vocabulary of Indian languages such as Sanskrit, into which words from Persian and Arabic were integrated.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Hindavi, taught in madrasas, had the grammar and vocabulary of Indian languages such as Sanskrit, with Persian and Arabic words integrated

questions.q: A shopkeeper in Srinagar in 2026 tells a tourist: 'Our pashmina shawl with its paisley motif is a purely Persian craft.' Using the chapter, give one point about the shawl's material and one about its embroidery, and then decide whether the shopkeeper is right.
questions.a: (1) Material: pashmina is woven from cashmere, a soft wool from the goats of Ladakh and Kashmir, so it rests on an Indian regional material and India's long weaving tradition, in which every region has its own speciality. (2) Embroidery: it shows a distinct Persian influence, with floral motifs, and the buteh or buta (paisley) motif is Persian; under the Mughals the shawls gained imperial patronage and became a symbol of nobility. (3) He is not right: the shawl is a blend of an Indian regional material and weaving with Persian-influenced embroidery, not a purely Persian craft.
s: Material: cashmere wool from goats of Ladakh and Kashmir, a regional Indian speciality
Embroidery: distinct Persian influence, floral motifs and the Persian buteh (paisley)
Decides he is wrong: an Indian material and weaving blended with Persian embroidery

questions.q: An exhibition panel reads: 'The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila was a loss of buildings only. The scholars carried on as before, and learning in India went on as if nothing had happened.' Evaluate the panel in four steps. (i) Besides calling it an immense cultural loss, what two further effects of the destruction does the chapter name? (ii) Using (i), explain why the panel's first two claims are wrong. (iii) Name two kinds of institutions where the tradition of learning persisted, one of them under Muslim rule, and say what that one taught. (iv) Decide how far the panel is right, and rewrite it in one sentence that fits the chapter.
questions.a: (i) It caused the dispersal of learned scholars, and an entire ecosystem was disrupted. (ii) The loss was not of buildings only: the community of learned scholars was scattered and the whole system of learning around the universities broke down, so the scholars could not carry on as before. (iii) Any one of gurukulas, mathas, temple schools, Buddhist viharas, Jain pallis or village pathashalas, and madrasas, which offered instruction in Arabic, Persian, Hindavi and Islamic studies. (iv) The panel is only partly right: the chapter says invasions disrupted India's educational landscape, yet the tradition of learning persisted from villages to temples, safeguarded by kings, saints, poets and scholars, often against great odds. A fair version: 'The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila was an immense loss that scattered scholars and disrupted a whole system of learning, yet learning persisted in smaller institutions across India.'
s: (i) Dispersal of learned scholars and an entire ecosystem disrupted
(ii) Uses (i): more than buildings were lost, and scholars could not carry on as before
(iii) One older institution (such as gurukulas or mathas) and madrasas with Arabic, Persian, Hindavi and Islamic studies
(iv) Partly right (learning persisted) but wrong that nothing happened, with a fair rewrite

questions.q: (a) Why did Persian become the language of administration and courtly culture in this period, according to the chapter? (b) Name any two kinds of texts it produced.
questions.a: (a) Because Persian was the language of the Mughals. (b) Any two of: histories, poetry, other texts that often helped preserve Indian knowledge from earlier times.
s: (a) Persian was the language of the Mughals
(b) Two kinds of texts, such as histories and poetry

questions.q:
A library in Kolkata plans a 2026 exhibition, 'Translations that built bridges', on the 13th to 17th centuries. It has five exhibits. E1: the Mahabharata translated into Bengali by a court-poet of the early 16th century. E2: the first Persian translation of Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati. E3: a Persian translation of Kalhana's Rajatarangini. E4: Persian translations of 52 Upanishads. E5: Persian poetry translated into Bengali.
(a) Who made the translation in E2, and how many Persian translations of the Lilavati does the chapter mention?
(b) Who is credited with the translations in E4, with whose help, and what later happened to them?
(c) Name the court-poet behind E1.
(d) The library has room for only three exhibits and wants to show that translation ran both into and out of Persian. Which three should it choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Abu al-Faiz ibn Mubarak, known as Faizi; the chapter mentions three Persian translations. (b) Dara Shikoh, with the help of learned scholars in Varanasi; the translations later reached Europe and influenced leading 19th-century philosophers and thinkers. (c) Kavindra Paramesvara. (d) E5 must be chosen, because it is the only exhibit that carries a text out of Persian. The other two should come from E2, E3 and E4, which carry Sanskrit texts into Persian. E1 does not serve the goal, because it is a translation from Sanskrit into Bengali and involves no Persian. A sound choice is E5, E4 and E2.
s: (a) Faizi, and three translations
(b) Dara Shikoh with scholars in Varanasi; the translations reached Europe and influenced 19th-century thinkers
(c) Kavindra Paramesvara
(d) Chooses E5 and two of E2, E3, E4, and explains why E1 does not fit

questions.q: (a) Name the scholar in the South whom the chapter credits with pioneering contributions to the study of calculus. (b) State the two world firsts that came from his work. (c) By what name are he and his followers known today, and until which century did they produce important works?
questions.a: (a) Madhava. (b) The series expansion for trigonometric functions, and an exact value of pi as an infinite series. (c) The Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics, which produced important works until the 19th century.
s: (a) Madhava
(b) Series expansion for trigonometric functions and pi as an infinite series
(c) The Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics, until the 19th century

questions.q:
Read the statements about clothing in this period.
I. Cotton, muslin and silk production went up.
II. The jama and pyjama were adopted in court, with variations for women.
III. The sari continued to be part of the wardrobe, with rich regional variations.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: (a) What did Greek travellers to India record about the way Indians dressed? (b) The angrakha, a robe-like upper garment, is believed to have evolved from Persian court fashion. Using (a), explain why the chapter would find its adoption in India natural, and state how it was changed in India.
questions.a: (a) They recorded the fine clothing, dyes, hairstyles, footwear (including high heels) and jewellery of Indians. (b) Their record shows that Indians had been very conscious of their attire since ancient times, so it was natural for them to experiment with styles they came across, such as Persian court fashion; the angrakha was adapted to Indian aesthetics and fabrics, and was worn by both men and women.
s: (a) Fine clothing, dyes, hairstyles, footwear including high heels, and jewellery
(b) Uses (a): attire-conscious since ancient times, so experimenting was natural; the angrakha was adapted to Indian aesthetics and fabrics

questions.q: Write three lines for the notebook of a cook in a 17th-century imperial kitchen. Each line must correctly use one fact the chapter gives: line 1 about spices, or curd and ghee; line 2 about naan; line 3 about what Akbar is said to have tried to change in his court's meals.
questions.a: Model answer: (1) 'Today I added cardamom, clove and black pepper to the dish; these spices are now used in the common people's kitchens too, and I marinated the meat in curd.' (2) 'The naan baked in the clay oven shows the Persian influence on our cooking.' (3) 'The emperor is said to want less meat cooked for himself and for his court, partly under the influence of the Jain and Hindu traditions of our time.' Any lines that use correct chapter facts earn the marks.
s: Line 1 correctly uses the spices (cardamom, clove, turmeric, coriander, black pepper) or curd for marination and ghee
Line 2 correctly shows naan, cooked in a clay oven, as a Persian influence
Line 3 correctly says Akbar tried to reduce meat consumption for himself and his court, partly under Jain and Hindu influence

questions.q: Krishnadevaraya's Vijayanagara appears in several sections of the chapter. (a) Music: whose fame reached his court, and what happened then? (b) Literature: what does the chapter say Krishnadevaraya did for poets? (c) Architecture: what did the empire see under his rule, and which city was its vibrant centre? (d) Education: what principle guided the Vijayanagara rulers, and how did it help learning continue? (e) Using (a) to (d), judge which of the chapter's three common patterns of the period (continuation of traditional practices, patronage from rulers, participation by people of all sections) Vijayanagara shows most clearly, and whether it also shows another.
questions.a: (a) The fame of Purandaradasa, the father of Carnatic music, reached Krishnadevaraya's court; he was eventually invited and became a part of it. (b) He patronised poets in south India. (c) A golden age of art, architecture and cultural revival; Hampi was a vibrant centre of urban planning and temple building. (d) Purvamaryade, following previously established practices of dharma and social norms; so the rulers supported temples and mathas, which let education continue. (e) Patronage from rulers is the clearest: the court invited Purandaradasa, patronised poets and built grand temples. It also shows continuation of traditional practices, since purvamaryade means following established practices and temple and matha learning carried on. A student who judges continuation of traditional practices the clearest (purvamaryade, temple and matha learning) and backs it from (a) to (d) also earns the mark.
s: (a) Purandaradasa's fame reached the court and he was invited and became part of it
(b) He patronised poets
(c) A golden age of art, architecture and cultural revival, with Hampi as its centre
(d) Purvamaryade: support for temples and mathas let education continue
(e) Judges one pattern as clearest (patronage or continuation) and supports it and a second pattern with evidence from (a) to (d)
